new_statements.quote: Accentuation. — Il existe en sara un accent tonique qui porte comme en français sur la dernière syllabe sonore du mot. Les voyelles brèves marquées du signe ˘ ne peuvent évidemment pas porter l'accent (1). — (1) « Il y a un accent et même un accent tonique qui, joint aux longues et aux brèves très marquées, ainsi qu'aux voyelles nombreuses et sonores, donne au sara parlé les apparences des langues de l'Europe méridionale, l'italien, l'espagnol et le portugais. » (Note de M. Clozel).
new_statements.translation: Accentuation. — There is in Sara a tonic accent which falls, as in French, on the last full (sonorous) syllable of the word. The short vowels marked with the breve sign obviously cannot bear the accent (1). — (1) 'There is an accent, indeed a tonic accent, which, together with the very marked long and short vowels and the numerous sonorous vowels, gives spoken Sara the appearance of the languages of southern Europe, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese.' (Note by M. Clozel).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent on the final syllable, skipping a final extra-short (breve-marked, reduced) vowel, i.e. on the last full-vowelled syllable of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: Extra-short (breve) vowels cannot carry the accent, so words ending in such a vowel are accented on the preceding syllable. Tone is not recognised at all by the author.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms elicited from a single speaker. CAVEATS: pre-phonemic 1897 description that does not recognise the three lexical tones every modern source describes; data from one displaced child semi-speaker (Ali, enslaved and taken to France) who had largely forgotten his language and re-learned it prompted with Barth's Bagirmi vocabulary; the 'sara' variety is not identified (born near the Bahr Sara; archive.org/Rosetta files the work under mwm). All modern accessible descriptions of Sar (Keegan 2014, Gotengaye & Keegan 2016, Keegan 1995, Fédry 1976) describe tone and length and are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Delafosse 1897 describes an unspecified 'sara' variety from a single child informant born near the Bahr Sara (archive.org/Rosetta Project files it under mwm = Sar, but it could equally be Mbay or another Sara Central lect); it is not a description of Sar/Sara Madjingay sensu stricto. The modern Sar sources read (Keegan 2014; Gotengaye & Keegan 2016) describe the Sar of Sarh/Koumra (sarr1246 proper) and treat Nar (Ethnologue: Sar dialect) separately. Thayer & Maraby 1966 'Sara' courses may actually be Ngambay-area material (dialogues reference Moundou).

Tucker & Bryan give the opposite placement, first syllable of disyllables, but at group level for all Bongo-Bagirmi languages and with Sara Mbai (mbay1241), not Sar, as the Sara variety analysed; no Majingai/Madjingay/Sar form is named anywhere the reprint's index reaches (six spelling queries, 0 hits). Glottolog's hh.bib codes the chapter's languages as Bongo, Sara Mbai, Bagirmi, Kresh, Baka. So this is an initial-stress statement for the group that contains Sar, not a Sar-specific one, and it differs from De…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Bongo-Bagirmi languages as a group (Western: Bagirmi Group and Sara Group; Central: Kresh Group, Kara; Eastern: Bongo Group), stress normally falls on the first syllable of a disyllabic word, and always does so when the second syllable has a semi-mute (reduced) vowel; stress shifts to the second syllable only when the first syllable has a central vowel (Stevenson's Bagirmi 'snake' example). The languages are also tonal, with tone both lexical and grammatical. The statement is made once for the whole chapter, not per language; its Sara data come from Sara Mbai.
new_statements.exceptions: Second-syllable stress when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Bagirmi k;lá 'snake', after Stevenson); initial stress is 'invariable' when the second syllable has a semi-mute vowel. Nothing on words longer than two syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 describe the Bongo-Bagirmi languages collectively (Western: Bagirmi Group, Sara Group; Central: Kresh Group incl. Yulu-Binga, Kara; Eastern: Bongo Group). Their Sara data are 'SARA MBAI' (Tucker's Paris informants; Stevenson's Sara Mbai Grammar MS.), i.e. Mbay (mbay1241), a sister of Sar within Sara proper; the catalog's tag 'Sara-Majingai' is not the book's wording (no Majingai/Madjingay spelling occurs in the reprint's index). The stress rule is therefore a group-level statement covering the Sara Group that contains Sar, not a statement made on Sar data. Delafosse 1897's 'sara' is Bagirmi-like (numerals, and his own remark that sara and baguirmien are 'deux dialectes d'une meme langue').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages (the Sara variety analysed is Sara Mbai, not Sar/Majingai; no Majingai form is indexed: feed query 'SARA MAJINGAY of' inauthor:Tucker -> 0 results): in disyllabic words stress normally falls on the first syllable, obligatorily so when the second syllable has a 'semi-mute' (reduced) vowel; occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable when the first syllable has a central vowel. Tone is lexical and grammatical, so this is a stress statement inside a tone-language description.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the snippet text available
new_statements.exceptions: second-syllable stress occasionally when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Stevenson's Bagirmi example k.la 'snake'); statement limited to disyllabic words
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter treats the Bongo-Bagirmi group as a whole; the Sara material is Sara Mbai (mbay1241; Tucker's work with Sara Mbai informants in Paris, snippet PT66), not Sar/Sara Majingai (feed query 'SARA MAJINGAY of' -> 0 hits). The statement therefore applies to Sar only by group membership.

readall_conflicts: Delafosse 1897 (existing statement) puts a French-like 'accent tonique' on the last full syllable of the word, from one displaced semi-speaker whose numerals are Bagirmi, not Sar. Tucker & Bryan 1966 put stress on the first syllable of disyllabic words (second syllable only when the first has a central vowel) for the whole Bongo-Bagirmi group, with Sara Mbai as the Sara variety analysed and Bagirmi supplying the exception example. The two placements are opposite (final vs initial), and neither source is securely about sarr1246: Delafosse's material is Bagirmi-like, Tucker & Bryan's is group-level with Mbay data. The Sar-specific sources held by the project (Gotengaye & Keegan 2016, Keegan 2014, Fedry 1976) describe three level tones and say nothing about stress. No new text was obtained, so nothing new conflicts with the catalog: the catalog's only record for Sar is Tucker & Bryan 1966 itself (classification weight-hedged, quoting sec. 2b 'Stress'), and the Google Books snippet of the 2017 reprint (PT71) reproduces that sentence word for word. The standing disagreement held by the project remains between the two existing statements, not between a source and the catalog: Tucker & Bryan (group-level, Bongo-Bagirmi, Sara Mbai as the Sara representative) put stress normally on the first syllable of disyllables with vowel-quality-conditioned exceptions, while Delafosse 1897 puts an 'accent tonique' on the last full ('sonore') syllable of the word; the first reader judged Delafoss…
